$schema_description: Course Study App — Production Lecture Additions Template. Defines Recommended Readings supplementary concepts and related exam questions & model answers for lecture slides across any course. All textual fields support full Markdown and LaTeX math ($inline$ or $$display$$ with double-escaped '\\'). The first slide entry below provides field-by-field instructions; subsequent entries show real examples.

markdown_and_latex_support.note: ALL TEXTUAL FIELDS SUPPORT FULL GITHUB-FLAVORED MARKDOWN AND KATEX MATH ($inline$ or $$display$$).
markdown_and_latex_support.mandatory_json_backslash_rule: CRITICAL: In JSON strings, the backslash '\' is the JSON escape character. Every LaTeX command MUST use double backslashes '\\'. For example, write '$\alpha$', '$\text{ms}$', '$$\frac{a}{b}$$', and '$O(M \times N)$'. Never write unescaped '\t' or '\f'. Escape literal dollar signs in prose as \$.
markdown_and_latex_support.code_and_math_rules: Use backticks (`$var`) exclusively for code, shell syntax, packet headers, and script variables; use dollar signs ($math$) exclusively for LaTeX math (never nest backticks in math). Never output raw HTML/MathML tags like <span class='katex'> or <math>. Escape literal dollar signs in prose as \$.

lecture_id: INSTRUCTION: Unique identifier string matching an 'id' from slides_index.json (e.g. 'lectures-module-1', 'lectures-net-arch', 'lectures-os-kernel'). Keep general and course-agnostic.
document: INSTRUCTION: The exact bare filename of the lecture PDF document (e.g. '01_Introduction.pdf', 'Lecture_Network_Architecture.pdf'). Do not include directory paths.
title: INSTRUCTION: The full human-readable title of this lecture slide set (e.g. 'Lecture 1: Systems Modeling, Measurement, and Performance Evaluation').

slides._comment: EXAMPLE 1: CONCRETE SLIDE WITH LITERATURE ADDITIONS AND RELATED MULTIPLE CHOICE EXAM QUESTION
slides.title: Comparing Two Alternatives: Motivation and Cases

literature_additions.concept: Paired vs. Unpaired Experimental Design & Variance Reduction
literature_additions.content:
In experimental systems evaluation, choosing between **paired** and **unpaired** observation models directly impacts statistical variance:

1. **Paired Observations**: Both alternatives are evaluated under identical benchmark workloads or identical test conditions (e.g. executing workload $W_i$ on both Alternative A and Alternative B). By subtracting pairwise $D_i = A_i - B_i$, workload-induced variance is mathematically eliminated, drastically narrowing the confidence interval.
2. **Unpaired Observations**: Trials are executed independently with non-corresponding inputs. This requires a two-sample $t$-test with pooled or Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which inherently exhibits higher variance.

Failing to pair when matching workloads are available inflates the required sample size by up to a factor of $2\times$ to $5\times$ for the same confidence level.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is **required** when applying a **paired $t$-test** to compare the performance of two computer system alternatives?

alternatives.text: The number of observations for Alternative A must equal the number of observations for Alternative B, and each pair must experience identical test conditions.
alternatives.lecture_explanation: A paired $t$-test computes the sample mean of differences $\bar{d} = \frac{1}{n}\sum (A_i - B_i)$. This operation mathematically requires a 1-to-1 correspondence ($n_A = n_B = n$) where external factors (cache state, input seed, memory footprint) are held constant across each pair to isolate the system difference.
alternatives.RR_addition: Pairing acts as an analytical **blocking factor** in experimental design: it converts homogeneous environment noise into a common-mode rejection, preventing environmental variance from inflating the experimental error term.

alternatives.text: The variances of the two alternatives must be proven equal using an $F$-test before subtraction.
alternatives.lecture_explanation: Testing for equality of variances is only relevant for **unpaired** samples using a pooled $t$-test. For paired samples, we analyze the single derived difference series $D_i = A_i - B_i$, so the individual sample variances of $A$ and $B$ do not need to be equal.
alternatives.RR_addition: The paired difference variable $D_i$ must only satisfy approximate normality for small sample sizes ($n < 30$), guaranteed by the Central Limit Theorem when $n \ge 30$.

abbreviations.phrase: Analysis of Variance (statistical technique for comparing means across multiple groups)

slides._comment: EXAMPLE 2: CONCRETE SLIDE WITH LITERATURE ADDITIONS AND RELATED WRITTEN EXAM QUESTION
slides.title: Discrete-Event Simulation (DES) Architecture

literature_additions.concept: Simulation Clock Advances & Event Queue Overhead
literature_additions.content:
In Discrete-Event Simulation (**DES**), the simulation clock does not advance continuously; instead, it jumps instantaneously from the timestamp of the current event to the scheduled timestamp of the next earliest event in the **Future Event List (FEL)**.

- **FEL Priority Queue**: Storing and retrieving events has algorithmic complexity that depends on the queue data structure. While simple binary heaps provide $O(\log N)$ insertion and deletion, high-throughput network simulations often utilize calendar queues or splay trees to achieve near $O(1)$ amortized event processing.
- **Event Routine Purity**: Event handlers must execute in zero simulation time. Modifying state variables must strictly occur via scheduled events to maintain deterministic reproducibility across runs.

questions.context: Consider a discrete-event simulator modeling a multi-core packet processing pipeline with an asynchronous Future Event List (FEL).

sub_questions.label: a
sub_questions.question: Explain how the global simulation clock advances in this architecture and contrast it with a time-stepped simulation model.
sub_questions.lecture_explanation: In a **Discrete-Event Simulation (DES)**, the simulation clock jumps discontinuously from the current event's completion timestamp directly to the timestamp of the next chronological event in the **Future Event List (FEL)**. Inactive periods with no events consume zero compute cycles. In contrast, a **time-stepped simulation** increments time by fixed intervals $\Delta t$, updating all state variables at every step regardless of whether any state transition occurred.
sub_questions.RR_addition: When the event density is sparse or non-uniform, DES offers orders-of-magnitude faster execution ($O(\text{events})$ vs $O(T / \Delta t)$). However, when state transitions occur at every cycle across thousands of concurrent nodes, priority queue maintenance costs ($O(\log N)$ per event) can degrade DES performance below fixed time-stepped execution.

sub_questions.label: b
sub_questions.question: What invariant must event handler execution adhere to regarding simulation time, and what problem arises if this invariant is violated?
sub_questions.lecture_explanation: Event handlers must execute in **zero simulation time**; that is, the simulation clock cannot advance while an event routine is running. If an operation takes non-zero simulated duration (e.g. packet transmission latency $L / C$), the start and completion must be scheduled as two separate discrete events. Violating this introduces non-deterministic race conditions and violates causal ordering in the event scheduler.
sub_questions.RR_addition: Maintaining strict causal purity allows parallel DES engines to employ optimistic time warp algorithms (Jefferson 1985) with anti-message rollbacks, or conservative null-message protocols (Chandy-Misra 1979) without deadlock.

abbreviations.phrase: Discrete-Event Simulation (computational modeling technique where state changes occur at discrete points in time)
Future Event List (chronologically ordered priority queue of pending simulation events)
